title: The Map of Unmade Roads
excerpt: An apprentice can draw a road that lasts one day, but every shortcut makes an existing path disappear.

sections.title: A Road for One Day
paragraphs: Anya could draw a road that existed for one day. At dawn the ink left the page and the path appeared on earth. At the next dawn it vanished, carrying away whatever had not reached the far side. Her master had taught her to use the gift only for emergencies: a bridge around a landslide, a trail to a missing shepherd, a way home for someone caught by floodwater. Every road had a cost. The ink came from stone ground with a memory of motion, and when one path was made, another nearby grew difficult to find.
Anya thought that warning meant a traveler might take a wrong turn. She had never seen a path disappear completely until the king summoned her.

The summons arrived while she was repairing a county map. King Aric wanted a road across the Blackglass Valley, where the mountain fell in sharp shelves and no ordinary track survived the winter. His army needed to cross before a rebel force reached the northern forts. He offered her a title, a house, and enough money to restore the mapmakers' hall. He did not ask what the road would take.

Anya traveled to the capital with her master, Sol, and a pack mule carrying paper, stone ink, and the survey instruments. At the palace she was shown a campaign map. The requested road was a straight line from the south gate to the valley's far ridge. It would save the army nine days. Sol placed a finger on the small villages along the old mountain route. 'Where do those people go if this new line takes theirs?'

The minister said the villages were almost empty. Anya asked to see the population ledger. The minister looked annoyed, then promised it tomorrow. That night a stable boy slipped a note under her door. His family lived in Sere, the first village marked almost empty. Seventy-six people lived there. They had stored enough food to last the winter and expected the old pass to remain open. If Anya's road displaced it, they would be trapped behind the ridge with no safe descent.

In the morning Anya asked the king for three days to survey the valley. He gave her one. She left with Sol and the stable boy, whose name was Pell. The palace expected her to choose the shortest line. She intended to find out who would pay for it.

sections.title: The Farmer's Field
paragraphs: Sol took Anya to the farm whose path he had once displaced. Its owner was a woman named Cera, with weathered hands and a laugh that arrived only after she had decided someone deserved to hear it. She recognized Sol before he reached the gate. 'You finally brought an apprentice to see your mistake,' she said.

The mine rescue had happened thirty years earlier. Cera's husband had been one of the trapped men. He survived the day because Sol drew a road through the rock. When he came home, the old track from their field to the market had lost its shape. For months Cera carried vegetables by a steep stream path, losing half her goods before she reached town. The miners were praised in songs. Her losses appeared in no account of the rescue. Sol had returned with tools and helped build steps by the stream, but he had never asked whether she considered the debt paid.

Cera served them barley tea. Anya asked if Sol should have left the miners in the mine. 'Of course not,' Cera said. 'But he could have told us the cost was coming. We might have stored food, found another way, sent a boy to warn the market. I was told after the road was drawn, when everyone else was celebrating. That was the part I couldn't forgive for years.'

Sol looked into his cup. He had told Anya the story as a warning about magic. Cera's version made it a warning about decisions. Anya wrote down the farm's route, the mine road, and the steps by the stream. She asked Cera to mark which path had vanished and how long it took to replace. The lines made a small ugly knot on the page. Anya wanted to smooth them, to make the map handsome. She left them as they were.
When they rose to go, Cera handed Anya a bundle of bread. 'If the king says there's no time to ask, remember that there will be time afterward to live with what you drew.'

sections.title: The Path That Vanished
paragraphs: Sere stood on a shelf of pale rock above the valley. Its stone houses leaned into the wind. Pell's grandmother, Dema, showed Anya a footpath marked by cairns and strips of red cloth. It led to a winter spring, the only water that did not freeze. Children had followed it for generations. A new road across the valley would run directly beneath the spring. Anya measured the distance twice. If the magic took the nearest existing path, the village might lose its water route.

Sol told her that in his youth he had drawn a rescue road after a mine collapse. Twelve miners reached daylight. The old track to a neighboring farm faded. For months the farmer could see it from her porch but could not walk it; every step turned her back toward home. Sol had spent a year finding another route for her. 'We count who is saved,' he said. 'We must count who is asked to wander.'

Anya tested a small line on a scrap of paper: a path only twenty paces long, from a fallen tree to the spring. At dawn it rose through the snow like a dark seam. Pell took one step on it and laughed. A moment later Dema called out. The red-cloth path behind the houses had vanished beneath smooth white ground. Her granddaughter tried to follow its remembered turns and walked into a stand of thorns she had never seen before. Anya erased the test line, but the old path did not return until the next dawn.

For one day the village had water only because Anya's little road reached the spring. She had made herself necessary by breaking what already worked. She hated how easily the act could be described as help.

At the capital, the minister received her measurements and said the village could use the army road for water after the soldiers passed. Anya explained that the army road would vanish the next dawn, and the old route might not return to the same place. He said the king had accepted the risk. Anya said the villagers had not. The minister reminded her she was a royal apprentice under a contract signed by Sol. Refusal could cost the hall its license.
Pell heard the threat. 'Draw it,' he told her privately. 'Then show them what happens. They're going to use someone else if you won't.'

Anya thought of a stranger drawing the road without seeing Sere. She asked Sol whether a map could hold two routes at once. He said the ink would not know which cost to take. Then he paused. There was an older method, forbidden since the Border War: draw the road with every neighboring path visible and let the ink divide the cost among them. It might spare Sere, but it could unsettle a whole region. Neither had enough maps to attempt it safely.

sections.title: The Names Beneath the Ink
paragraphs: Mira brought Anya into a sealed room beneath the library, where maps from the Border War hung behind screens. The forbidden divided-cost method had been used there. At first glance the maps looked miraculous: roads crossing marshes, passes through cliffs, bridges over water. Then Mira lifted each screen. Beneath the bright ink were small red marks recording paths that had become unreliable in exchange. A miller lost the ford his family used for flour. A village lost the footbridge to its burial ground. In one valley, children could see the path to school but found themselves circling the same tree whenever they tried to walk it.

The old mapmakers had split the cost so thinly that no single loss seemed severe. The army celebrated a network of new roads. Thousands of ordinary journeys became harder, and nobody could tell which drawn line had caused which failure. The court closed the method after a winter in which three families froze while looking for a home they could see across a field.
'Why keep the maps?' Anya asked.
'Because a ban can be forgotten,' Mira said. 'A record of who suffered is harder to dismiss.'

They searched for a safer version of the method anyway. Anya was afraid the king would force another apprentice to attempt it. She found a notation in the margin of a war map: roads drawn on empty ground disturbed fewer paths, but empty ground on a royal map was often occupied by people the crown had not counted. Anya thought of Sere's false population. The magic itself might not be cruel; the mapmakers' ignorance gave it room to be.

Mira showed her a survey of the quarry, dated before the war. It marked an old workers' track mostly hidden by rockfall. Anya ran her finger along it to the ford. It was longer than the king's line, but it had once carried carts. If the villages agreed to reopen it, ordinary stonework could do what dangerous ink had promised. She copied the survey and asked Mira to bring it to the festival with the village rolls.

sections.title: The Missing Ledger
paragraphs: The population ledger arrived two days late and had been altered. Sere had become sixteen people, not seventy-six. Three other villages had been marked abandoned. Anya recognized the same clerk's hand on every correction. She took the ledger to the palace library, where earlier copies were stored on vellum. The old numbers matched Pell's account. The minister had not merely ignored the villages; he had erased them to make the road appear cheap.

The royal librarian, Mira, helped her compare the maps. Mira's brother commanded the northern fort and had written that the rebel force was months away, not nine days. The army road was intended to move troops quickly, but the emergency had been exaggerated. When Anya asked why, Mira showed her a trade map. A straight road across the valley would let Aric seize a mine before the regional lords could claim it. The king's ministers called it a defensive campaign. The people near the mine called it conquest.

Anya could expose the false ledger, but the king might simply find another mapmaker. She needed a way to make the truth visible to people whose decisions mattered. Mira suggested a public survey. The palace had announced that Anya would display her proposed road at the spring festival. She could show more than a line. If she brought the old routes and the names of the people using them, the king would have to reject the map in front of his own citizens.

They copied the village rolls through the night. Pell drew wells and lambing grounds that official maps omitted. Sol added paths he had walked as a boy. Dema sent a list of the seventy-six people in Sere, each with a mark beside those who could not travel quickly: infants, elders, a man with a broken leg. Anya made the map large enough to hang across the square. The requested road ran in black ink. The paths it endangered ran in red.

On festival morning the minister ordered her to remove the red lines. Anya refused. Guards approached the frame. Mira called out the names of the villages in a voice trained to carry through library halls. People stopped to listen. A merchant recognized the route he used to buy wool. A woman from another village asked why her family's bridge had been marked empty. The guards hesitated as the crowd gathered around the map.
King Aric arrived under a blue canopy. He looked at the red lines for a long time. 'Can you draw the road without losing them?' he asked.
'Not with the maps I have,' Anya said. 'And not by pretending the people on them aren't there.'

The king ordered the minister to explain the altered ledger. The minister said the clerk had made a mistake. Pell stepped forward and recited the original count from memory. The king dismissed the minister from the square, but he did not withdraw the order. He gave Anya until sunset to propose another route. Anya understood: a ruler could punish a lie and still want what it had promised him.

sections.title: The King and the Empty Valley
paragraphs: At sunset, after the public map had stirred the square, Aric summoned Anya alone. He had dismissed the minister, but his own seal was on the order to cross the valley. He stood before a window overlooking rooftops and asked why she thought he wanted the mine.
'Because the trade map says it will make you rich,' Anya answered.
'It will make the northern forts independent of foreign iron. The rebels have burned two supply convoys. My commanders say another winter without that mine will cost soldiers their hands and feet.'

Anya had been ready to treat the mine as greed. Aric's answer did not make the plan just, but it explained why he feared delay. She showed him Pell's letter and the unaltered village ledger. Aric said the minister had told him Sere was nearly deserted. He could have checked. Anya did not say it aloud. His silence suggested he knew.
'You can draw a road tomorrow,' he said. 'I have seen you do it.'
'Yes.'
'And if you refuse, I can command Sol.'
'Yes.'
'Then why are we still talking?'

Anya set Cera's map on his table, the knot of old and new paths. She told him about the miners saved and the farm made unreachable. Aric read the red marks without comment. She said she would draw a rescue road if soldiers were trapped tomorrow. She would not draw one to make a campaign faster while the people in its path had been counted as empty.
The king looked toward the northern horizon. 'A ruler is told to think of the greatest number.'
'Then count them accurately,' Anya said.

He could have ended the conversation with a guard at the door. Instead he asked how long a normal road would take. She showed him the quarry survey. He rejected it as too slow, then asked her to bring the villagers and the engineers by morning. He had not agreed. He had made room for a better argument. Anya left knowing that if the argument failed, refusal would still be hers to make.

sections.title: The Valley's Own Map
paragraphs: Anya returned to Sere with the older maps. Dema spread them across the table while Pell fetched villagers from neighboring shelves. They marked every route used in winter and every one that had failed in spring floods. Their knowledge did not fit on the palace sheet. A road was a relation among homes, water, animals, and weather, not a line between two military points.

By midday they found a longer way to the far ridge: an abandoned quarry track and a shallow ford, repaired in stages. It would take the army six days, not one. It required stonework, wages, and the consent of two villages. It would not need magic. Anya brought the proposal to Aric. He called it slow. She said slow enough to keep the paths that fed his people.

The king's advisers argued that delay would cost lives if the rebellion advanced. Mira produced her brother's letter from the fort, sealed and dated. The danger was real but not immediate. Aric read it twice. He asked why the letter had not reached his desk. Nobody answered. He looked at the dismissed minister's empty chair.

Aric agreed to send surveyors and builders to the quarry route, but he wanted Anya to draw a small road for the first supply wagons. She considered the ford. A short path around the unstable bank could save the builders two days. The nearest existing trail belonged to shepherds who used it only in summer. They were present at the meeting. Anya asked them what would happen if the trail was lost for a day. They could wait, one said, if the wagons carried stone to repair the ford they would use for years. They asked to see the exact line and the date before agreeing.
Anya marked the temporary line with the shepherds watching. They agreed to return at dawn to witness the drawing, then to check the old trail when the magic faded.

The mapmakers' hall did not receive the grand royal grant the minister had promised. Aric paid for the survey and reopened the hall's license under a new rule: before any magic road was drawn, the paths at risk had to be named, and the people who used them had to be heard. Sol said the rule would be difficult to enforce. Anya said it was a beginning.

sections.title: Stones for Tomorrow
paragraphs: The builders discovered the old quarry track under a skin of moss and loose scree. Its foundations were sound, but the ford had to be raised. The two villages on either side disagreed over who would supply stone. Aric's officials offered wages to one and compulsory labor to the other. Dema refused to let the work begin under those terms. Anya had promised the road would be made by agreement; she would not use her magic to hurry people past a new injustice.

Pell and the engineers counted available stone. One village had quarry tools, the other had teams of mules. They revised the contract so both were paid for what they supplied. The soldiers who would use the route first were assigned to carry material as well as guard it. The commander protested that troops were not laborers. Aric, present for the inspection, asked whether a soldier's strength would be harmed by moving stone. The commander stopped protesting. Anya saw that a king could change a day's work with one question. She wished he had asked more before ordering the first line across the valley.

A storm delayed them. Rain filled the ford and washed away the first foundation. The engineer wanted to move the crossing upstream through a pasture. The shepherds showed him where the ground stayed firm in flood. Their route added half a mile and spared the pasture. On the second attempt the stones held. Anya drew the temporary magic road at dawn, and the supply wagons began crossing toward the builders.

Pell waited by the old shepherd trail, ready to test it when the magic ended. Anya asked him to record what he found. A future mapmaker should know whether the road had worked without leaving another path lost.

sections.title: When the Ink Dried
paragraphs: The temporary road around the ford lasted from dawn to dawn. Anya stood at its edge near midnight while the last supply cart crossed. The driver was a young soldier who had never seen magic ink become ground. He asked whether the road would disappear all at once. Anya said it would fade from the far side first. He urged his mule forward. One wheel struck a loose stone and jammed. The soldiers pushed, but the cart was loaded with tools for the builders and would not move.

Anya could not extend the magic by adding more ink. A second road might steal another path from the shepherds. She asked the driver which tools were essential by morning. He chose the chisels and a box of nails. They unloaded them onto the far bank. The cart still would not shift. At the ford, Pell called for the mule team from Sere. Dema's neighbors arrived with ropes and a practiced knowledge of stuck wheels. The mule pulled while the soldiers lifted. The cart lurched free with an hour to spare.

The driver wanted to thank Anya for the road. She pointed to the people coiling ropes and gathering scattered tools. The road had helped, but it had not crossed itself. He thanked them too. At dawn the dark seam in the earth thinned into ordinary wet grass. Anya watched the shepherd trail take shape again. Pell walked its first bend and returned, proving it led where it had before.

Sol arrived with breakfast. He told Anya that when he was young, he had wanted every road he drew to be remembered as a miracle. Now he was proudest of the ones people could forget once they had served their purpose. Anya ate warm bread and looked at the builders laying stone for a path that would not vanish. The magic had made time. The people had decided what to do with it.

sections.title: The Road Through Memory
paragraphs: Before the guild hearing, Anya visited the valley with Mira to check the roads that had been marked on the king's map as empty. They found a trail so narrow it looked like a crack in the grass. It led to a clearing where stones carried the names of people buried during the Border War. A family from Sere came every year with flowers. No tax ledger recorded the path because no goods moved along it. A map made only for trade would never show why it mattered.

Mira knelt beside one stone. Her grandmother was buried there. She had been a messenger who crossed the valley when roads were closed, carrying letters between people on opposite sides of the war. 'The court called this ground unused,' Mira said. 'They meant it made no money.'

Anya drew the trail on her field sheet. She marked the stones and the dates the family visited. The line would be visible to future mapmakers, though she worried a future king might use it to find the clearing for a different purpose. Mira suggested keeping sensitive details in the village copy and marking the royal sheet only as a protected route. Anya had thought honesty required every fact to be visible to everyone. She began to understand that a true map could also protect people from those who would misuse it.

On the way back they met three soldiers surveying the same ridge. Their captain wanted to know why two women were measuring a grave path. Anya showed him her seal. He said the army needed a route and asked whether memories would stop a rebel blade. Mira answered that her brother held the fort and had asked for supplies, not a road over his grandmother's grave. The captain recognized her name and lowered his eyes. He had never seen the clearing on his own map. He asked for a copy of the protected-route mark so his surveyors would not erase it by mistake.

At the guild hearing Anya included the encounter in her testimony. The line on a map could keep a road from being built as surely as it could make one appear. That, she decided, was also part of a mapmaker's work.

sections.title: The Apprentice's Seal
paragraphs: After the quarry contract was signed, the guild summoned Anya to answer for displaying the red paths at the festival. Two senior mapmakers said she had exposed private routes and embarrassed the king. They were more troubled by the embarrassment than by the altered village ledger. Sol sat beside her and let her speak for herself.

Anya admitted she had drawn the twenty-pace test road without first asking everyone in Sere. The village had lost its spring path for a day. She brought Dema's written account and Pell's measurements. She had told the story publicly because she wanted the guild to change how tests were approved. One senior mapmaker asked why she was confessing an error nobody had charged her with. Anya said a map could be accurate about distance and still dishonest about who had to walk it.

The guild voted to reprimand her for the test and to preserve her festival map in its archive. They declined to adopt the listening rule until the king issued it. Sol smiled at that contradiction. Institutions, he told Anya afterward, often needed to be led to the right door twice: once to see it, once to walk through. Anya did not find the saying comforting. She wanted the next apprentice to need less courage than she had.

She proposed a practical change. Each magic-road request would have a second page with the existing routes around it, signed by people who used them. If no one could be found to sign, the mapmaker would record the search and the reason for drawing anyway. Emergencies would remain possible; silence would no longer be mistaken for consent. The guild accepted the form on a trial basis. Anya made the first stack herself and sent copies to village schools, where children could correct the paths adults had left out.

Pell sent back one of those forms with a sketch of Sere. He had marked the winter spring, the new quarry route, and an old path to a berry slope that appeared on no official sheet. Beside it he wrote: My grandmother says this one matters in autumn. Anya added it to the regional map. It was a small line. She knew better than to call it unimportant.

sections.title: The Other Side of the Map
paragraphs: The road to the northern fort changed trade as soon as the first stones were laid. A baker from Sere began sending bread with the supply wagons. A family by the old pass worried that travelers would stop buying from them. Anya had saved their path from magic but could not keep every consequence of a new road from reaching them. She went to the family's inn and listened. The owner, Faris, showed her a ledger of guests who had stayed during winter storms. His house had been a shelter as much as a business. If the quarry route carried everyone away, he would struggle to keep it open.

Anya brought Faris to the builders' meeting. The commander said the army could not choose a route to support one inn. Faris agreed. He asked only that the old pass remain marked as an emergency refuge and that the supply crews know his signal fire. The commander added it to the march orders. Mira arranged for the fort to pay Faris to keep fuel and blankets ready during the cold season. It did not replace every lost guest. It gave a necessary service a name and a budget.

Pell wrote the signal fire on his survey. Anya asked how he would mark the bakery, the spring, and the burial path without crowding the sheet. He said he would make separate maps for different travelers. One map could guide wagons, another families in winter, another people looking for the clearing where their ancestors lay. None would be the only true map. Anya had spent her apprenticeship learning to draw one definitive page. Pell's answer made her laugh at how much she still had to learn.

Later, a messenger from the fort arrived with news that the rebel force had accepted talks. The new road had not won a battle. It had kept supplies moving while people negotiated. Aric announced this as proof of his foresight. Anya thought of the minister's false ledger and the first line she had refused to draw. A safer road had been made because many people had insisted on being counted, not because one ruler had seen the whole valley from his window.

At the opening ceremony, the king invited Anya to cut a ribbon at the ford. She gave the knife to Dema, whose village had carried stone and argued for fair wages. Dema cut the ribbon in one clean motion and handed the knife back. No magic flared. The crowd crossed on ordinary feet. Anya watched Faris speak with a soldier about winter blankets and Pell sketch a turn in the path. The road had begun to belong to the people who would use it. That was the only kind of completion she trusted.

The village copies did not always agree. One farmer marked a shortcut across his field; his neighbor said the shortcut crossed a planted strip and should be closed in spring. Pell drew both accounts and the dates when the path was usable. Anya had once thought a disagreement made a map unreliable. Now she saw that pretending agreement would be the greater error. Travelers could choose a route with open eyes when the page showed who maintained it, what season changed it, and whom to ask before crossing. The map grew less elegant and more helpful with every conversation.

sections.title: The Unmade Road
paragraphs: In late spring Anya visited the quarry route. Children from Sere were counting the new stone steps; a shepherd corrected their numbers while pretending not to enjoy it. The path to the winter spring still wound beneath red cloth and small cairns. Dema had added one more cairn where Anya's test road had crossed it, a reminder that even a short line could matter.

Pell walked with her to the ridge. He had decided to train as a surveyor. He said palace maps were too empty and wanted to draw the things officials tended to leave out. Anya gave him a fresh sheet. He drew the spring first, then the houses, then the paths between them. Only at the end did he add the boundary of the king's land.

From the ridge, the Blackglass Valley looked almost easy to cross. A ruler looking down from a high tower might still ask for a straight road through it. Anya could imagine drawing that road now more clearly than before. She also knew the names it would pass through. Her gift had not become less powerful because she had learned to pause. It had become more useful.
She wrote the date beside the ford, then left room at the edge of the page for the paths the next traveler might know better than she did.

She folded Pell's map and put it beside her own. The quarry road turned around the valley instead of cutting across it, adding miles no one could hide. Far below, wagons moved slowly over the new ford. They would still be moving tomorrow. That, Anya thought, was worth the distance.
